item.title: When Your Parents Become Your Roommates
item.description:
Family Dynamics

When Your Parents Become Your Roommates

How can we create new paradigms instead of falling into old patterns.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • As the older population ages, self-care for caregivers is a popular topic in research and media.
  • However, renegotiating identities and relationships may be the greatest challenge.
  • The need for autonomy and independence doesn't diminish with age.
  • Consciously creating new ways of relating and cohabitating may be the ticket to success.

As people live longer and the older population grows, there are increasing conversations about adult children becoming caregivers for their parents. This can present significant psychological, emotional, and financial challenges, and, as a result, self-care for caregivers is a popular topic in research and media.

Source: By Samantha Stein

However, when elderly parents move in with their adult children, the greatest psychological challenge may not be caregiving. Instead, it could be renegotiating identities and relationships that have existed for decades.

Old Roles and Autonomy

Even after decades of independence, living with parents again can reactivate familiar parent-child dynamics and old roles. The adult child can revert to being the responsible offspring—the loving, supportive parent can become critical or directive, and the independent adult suddenly feels they need permission.

Furthermore, parents need to feel in control of their own lives; the need for autonomy doesn’t expire with age. Just because someone has diminishing abilities doesn’t mean they don't need control over their own lives. Older adults, just like anyone with disabilities, retain a fundamental need for self-determination. Even well-intentioned assistance can undermine someone’s sense of competence and control.

A New Vision Called Roommates

What if the healthiest approach to intergenerational cohabitation is not to treat the arrangement as an extension of the parent-child relationship? Perhaps the healthiest arrangement isn't a return to the family home of childhood but the creation of an entirely new household, with three autonomous adults negotiating how to live together.

Current research on autonomy and intergenerational relationships supports this idea–I’m taking it a step further. I’m inviting everyone involved to consciously create new relationships and explore what the relationships might look like. To have discussions that involve negotiating privacy, household responsibilities, schedules, or boundaries, rather than relying on assumptions or the old way of doing things.

This can mean exploring the difference between caring and caretaking, how adult children can offer practical support without assuming authority over their parents’ lives, or surrendering authority over their own. For example, noticing a parent may need assistance with a task but asking before jumping in. The challenge isn’t learning how to be a good offspring or parent again–it’s about creating new ways of relating that fit today’s reality. It’s about creating a roommate paradigm that works for everyone and can be regularly renegotiated as circumstances change. And perhaps, in the process, discovering a new kind of closeness that wasn't possible within the old roles.

item.title: Chronic Back Pain Is Linked to a Sense of Personal Identity
item.description:
Chronic Pain

Chronic Back Pain Is Linked to a Sense of Personal Identity

New research answers the question of why chronic low back pain feels so personal.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Pain signals originate in the brain, but research has only recently begun to identify its neural circuitry.
  • The DMN is a group of interconnected brain regions involved in identity formation and internal narrative.
  • With chronic pain, DMN activity indicates the brain is continuously engaged with internal self-monitoring.
  • New research recommends approaches to disentangle the physical sensation of chronic pain from a sense of self.
Source: Mohamed Hassan from Pixabay

According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the most prevalent chronic pain condition and the leading cause of disability worldwide. In 2020, low back pain affected 619 million people globally.[1]

Low back pain (LBP) describes pain between the lower edge of the ribs and the buttock, and it can be acute (short-term) or chronic. Chronic low back pain (cLBP) is defined by pain that lasts more than 3 months. Chronic pain tends to have ongoing adverse effects on mental and emotional well-being, as well as overall quality of life. It can limit work and recreational activities, as well as engagement with family and friends.

Chronic low back pain can be specific or non-specific. Specific cLBP is pain caused by a particular disease or structural issue related to the spine, or when the pain radiates from another part of the body to that area. Non-specific cLBP is when no disease or structural reason to explain the pain can be identified. Importantly, cLBP is non-specific in approximately 90% of cases. Yet treatments for cLBP—and non-specific cLBP in particular—often fail to provide significant relief.

The Connection Between Chronic Pain and Sense of Self

Pain signals originate in the brain, but research has only recently begun to identify its specific neural circuitry. The Default Mode Network (DMN) is a grouping of interconnected regions of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes of the brain that becomes active when we are thinking about ourselves and our identity or reflecting on internal thoughts and feelings—rather than focusing on the outside world. It’s thought to be involved in building and maintaining a coherent sense of self, and, as such, it is connected to identity formation, self-reflection, and internal narrative.[2]

Ordinarily, the DMN (also known as the “self network”) effectively shuts down when a person focuses on an external stimulus or task. However, for people afflicted with chronic pain, the DMN fails to deactivate, meaning the brain is continuously engaged with internal distress and self-monitoring.[3] This activity in the DMN helps explain why chronic pain is rarely just a physical sensation.

A newly published study in the British Journal of Anaesthesia further demonstrates why typical symptom-based approaches to chronic pain are often ineffective and suggests that targeting the DMN may be a better way to treat cLBP.[4] Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine studied 114 cLBP patients while they performed a standard leg raise test to intentionally precipitate a spike in back pain while they measured blood flow in the brain using a specialized functional MRI technique. As a control, they also tested how the same patients' brains responded to a painful but harmless heat stimulus to the calf, comparable to touching a hot stove.

The results indicated that movement-generated pain associated with chronic pain activated the DMN—providing evidence that the experience of chronic pain is embedded in the sense of self, with consequent effects on one’s identity. In contrast, when the participants were subjected to the painful sensation of heat, their DMN shut down—consistent with the brain’s usual response to acute pain, allowing the brain to focus entirely on the external threat.

This study provides neuroscientific evidence of how, under the influence of cLBP, present moment experience is soiled, not only by the feeling of pain, but by rumination and rapid-fire catastrophizing cognitions that drive repetitive, negative thought loops, such as "Will this pain ever stop?” “What if it gets worse?" “How will it affect my plans today?” and “What does this say about who I am?” The deviation-amplifying dynamic precipitates emotional dysregulation, most often in the forms of anxiety and depression, escalates the suffering attached to the pain signal, and completes the vicious circle by exacerbating the subjective intensity of the pain.

Implications for Treatment

These results suggest that treatment approaches that help people separate the physical experience of chronic pain from their sense of self can lead to reductions to pain intensity and may well be more effective than traditional symptom-based approaches. Such approaches include mindfulness and psychedelic-assisted treatment whose mechanisms of action impact the mind-body-spirit continuum.

Mindfulness is a range of techniques focused on cultivating radical acceptance and non-judgmental awareness of internal and external present-moment experience that considerable research shows can measurably reduce the subjective experience of pain. Psychedelics such as psilocybin are known to alter thought processes by loosening rigid, repetitive thought patterns, expanding perspectives, and inspiring spiritual experiences—including creating or deepening a sense of connection with what is beyond the self. Although the specific mechanisms of psychedelic-assisted treatments remain uncertain, the action of these substances seems to enhance neuroplasticity, altering neural pathways, cognition, affect, and behavior—in ways that increase psychological flexibility.

All of this points toward the value of fundamentally shifting the direction of chronic pain interventions—from attempting to eliminate the pain (which is generally unrealistic) to helping people change their relationship to their pain. When this can be accomplished in ways that separate the experience of pain from one’s personal identity, it can dramatically decrease mental-emotional-spiritual suffering and meaningfully improve quality of life.

item.title: Let the Sunshine In, Feeling Good Takes Deliberate Practice
item.description:
Awe

Let the Sunshine In, Feeling Good Takes Deliberate Practice

To regularly experience positive emotions, we need to train.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Reducing distress and building joy are partly independent; each deserve our attention.
  • Positive affect treatment trains anticipation, savoring, and learning to strengthen reward processing.
  • Repeated positive experiences reshape the brain, making safety, joy, and connection easier to access.
  • Awe can be especially potent. It stretches our worldview and invites new meaning.

Strengthening Happiness Muscles

Since 2010, I have worked with people experiencing trauma, loss, and moral distress. I have witnessed what data shows: reducing distress and experiencing goodness are two separate endeavors.

Someone can cut their PTSD symptoms dramatically and still experience anhedonia (diminished positive affect). Someone can learn to manage panic attacks and still be waiting for life to begin. Conversely, someone can carry significant psychological distress and still have a connected, meaningful, joy-filled life.

We can strengthen our capacity to experience the good.

Bad Is Stronger than Good, Unless We Practice

Negativity bias kept our species alive. Survival favored the ancestor who mistook a shadow for a predator over the one who mistook a predator for a shadow. Social psychologist Roy Baumeister and colleagues (2001) summarized decades of research in five words: "Bad is stronger than good."

For example, a compliment evaporates by lunch while a criticism replays all week. Positive experiences can shape us, but we need to notice, savor, and learn from them.

A Treatment Built Around Reward

Most psychotherapy for depression and anxiety targets negative emotion. Positive affect treatment, developed by Michelle Craske, Alicia Meuret, and colleagues, targets the reward system directly.

In a 2026 randomized clinical trial of 98 adults with severely low positive affect and depression or anxiety, 15 sessions of this treatment produced greater reductions in anxiety and depression than a treatment focused on reducing negative affect. The advantage held at one-month follow-up (Meuret and colleagues, 2026). Positive affect treatment breaks down the process of cultivating pleasant emotions into three steps:

  1. Plan for and anticipate positive emotions like joy, gratitude, awe, and pride. When we plan pleasurable activities and anticipate the reward, we get a dopamine rush and strengthen our ability to respond spontaneously and creatively instead of reacting in threat response patterns (Fredrickson, 2001).
  2. Enjoy and savor these experiences. It’s not enough to have these experiences. To change, we can actively engage them, notice what we like about them, and recall vivid aspects of the experience.
  3. Learn. Once we experience support, we can notice what was significant and replicate this experience. This includes allowing ourselves to feel pride for our growing happiness muscles.
article continues after advertisement

Repetition matters. The more often we experience safety, joy, connection, pride, and awe, the more available those states become, and the more readily we spot opportunities for them in our environment. We can train the brain to pay attention, savor, and learn, and it becomes easier to do so. We don't need to practice four hours a day. It's better to practice in small, sustainable ways throughout the day.

Awe May Be Especially Important

Awe is a positive emotion that may be especially important to cultivate. Drs. Dacher Keltner and Jonathan Haidt (2003) describe awe as our response to vastness that exceeds our current mental frameworks and asks us to accommodate something new. Awe works on two levels. It feels good, and it reorganizes how we understand ourselves and our place in the world.

In a 2025 randomized controlled trial, 68 adults living with long COVID completed four courses on awe. They then practiced finding brief moments of awe in everyday life, a few times a day; they reported a 17 percent decrease in depressive symptoms, a 12 percent decrease in stress, and a 16 percent increase in well-being— compared with a waitlisted group (Monroy and colleagues, 2025). In one of my favorite awe studies, Dr. Surm and colleagues (2020) showed that individuals who attempted to experience awe during nature walks had significantly improved well-being, compared with those who walked in nature without such attempts.

Addressing Barriers to Happiness

In my work with veterans and first responders, savoring often feels foreign at first. Mission focus trained them to scan for what could go wrong. In psychotherapy, we work together to redirect disciplined vigilance towards what is going right (for instance, can you discipline yourself to notice good drivers?)

We often need to address barriers to experiencing happiness. Notice any protests your mind has: Don't feel happy because if you do ______. For instance, many individuals I have worked with feel guilty over experiencing positive emotions and think they "don't deserve to be happy." If it didn't have to be about deserving, can you see how experiencing some positivity might help you show up more fully for those you love and want to serve?

article continues after advertisement

Others I have worked with who have survived hard things feel uneasy when joy arrives, fearing a traumatic crash. It is true that everything we love changes, and we can't hold on to the emotional highs. We have a choice: Do we want a life with only lows? Or do we want a full life, with highs and lows?

An Invitation to Practice

I challenge you to:

  • Plan and anticipate: Find one small opportunity for growth or service today, and let yourself look forward to it.
  • Savor: When something good happens, pause for 20 seconds and replay it, recalling all the juicy details.
  • Learn: Before sleep, recall one moment in your day you want to remember. Ask yourself, “What did I do that helped this happen?”

Access moments of A.W.E. (Monroy and colleagues, 2025) in your life through these steps:

  • Attention: Give full, undivided attention to things you appreciate, value, or find meaning. (Falling leaves? A genuine smile?)
  • Wait: Slow down and pause.
  • Exhale and expand: Amplify whatever sensations you are experiencing.

Hold onto the good you experience through the exercise Dr. Rick Hanson (2013) developed called "H.E.A.L.":

  • Have a positive experience by noticing one that is already there, or creating one.
  • Enrich it. Sustain and intensify it, letting it grow.
  • Absorb it. Sense it sinking in and becoming part of us.
  • Link it. Hold the positive experience alongside older painful material, keeping the positive in the foreground.
article continues after advertisement

Whatever you try, notice what shifts. Can you start to build happiness muscles?

Your distress and your flourishing each deserve attention. You can learn to carry grief with acceptance and compassion, and feel the sun on your face, all in the same afternoon.

What would it look like to give the good in your life the same attention you give threats?

Where might awe already be waiting for you?

item.title: One Pill Can Kill
item.description:
Parenting

One Pill Can Kill

How to talk with young people about drug risks.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Drug overdose deaths in the U.S. increased between 2017 and 2023 and began to decrease between 2023 and 2024.
  • There is still work to do to educate youth on the dangers of counterfeit pills and powders.
  • Parents and other trusted adults need effective strategies for how to talk about drug dangers.
  • Trusted relationships with young people make hard conversations easier to have.

A few years ago, I received an urgent text from the mother of a client. The call that followed is every parent’s worst nightmare: “She is dead.” My heart sank; stunned and in disbelief, I asked, “What do you mean?” This incredible 25-year-old had not had issues with drugs, other than occasional use with friends, and had worked so hard to improve her mental health. She had her whole life ahead of her until a pill given to her by a friend killed her. I promptly cancelled my clients for the day, went home, hugged my teenage boys tight, then had a heartfelt conversation about the dangers of pills, powders, and plants.

detail-of-fingers-holding-tablet-near-mouth
Source: Vecteezy/used with permission

According to the CDC’s National Vital Statistics Report (2024), drug overdoses in the U.S. jumped from 70,715 in 2017 to 106,352 in 2023. The top killers were fentanyl, methamphetamine, and cocaine, in that order. The good news is that for youth age 15-24, overdose death rates declined by 37% between 2023 and 2024. According to the CDC (2025) this decrease has been attributed to multiple factors, including the increased accessibility of naloxone (Narcan), improved access to evidence-based mental health and addiction treatment, systemic efforts to decrease the drug supply, and public health educational efforts by both government and private organizations.

One such organization, partnering with hundreds of other public and private organizations to promote drug awareness, is Song for Charlie. Charlie’s sudden death in 2020, from a single fentanyl-laced pill designed to look exactly like a Percocet, led his shattered parents to channel their profound grief into a public health crusade.

A research survey by Song for Charlie found trends that can help inform how to reach young people so they understand the fatal dangers of fake prescription and other drugs:

  • Kids decide whether a pill is safe based on who handed it to them, not what could be in it.
  • More than 1 in 5 young adults think they could spot a fake pill just by looking at it.
  • Stress is one of the top reasons young people give for why their peers misuse pills, right up there with getting high and having fun.
  • Teens (especially older teens) know way more about fentanyl than they used to and understand it can be lethal.
  • Parents report having conversations about drug use, while young people are not nearly as likely to report the same.

What Can Parents Do for Greater Impact?

Aside from parents staying informed about the dangers of drugs (dea.gov is a great place to start), how we approach conversations with young people can improve our impact. Based on collective research, and years of experience working with adolescents, there are a few helpful principles to keep in mind.

Lead with your relationship.

Tough conversations are much more likely to be well-received and impactful when built upon regular, positive interactions. For harder moments, build trust by listening to one another, respecting room for differing perspectives, and exchanging information while honoring the autonomy of young people. When they feel our interest is in their growth, progress, and personal well-being, rather than focusing exclusively on consequences, they are more likely to share and listen.

Encourage the exploration of pros and cons.

All decisions have their pros and cons. Weighing a cost-benefit analysis when thinking about where young people stand on any number of issues or situations can help to create a balanced perspective, psychological flexibility, and some healthy internal conflict. Whenever possible, we want to try to reroute conflict from between us and them to within them.

It can be helpful to start with the pros, however much we may dislike them. When young people seek or receive offers to use drugs, there is a payoff. For some, it is momentary escape, relief, a sense of belonging, or simply pleasure or fun. If we cannot validate these perceived upsides, the conversation may end before we can highlight the dangers.

It can feel hard to be dialectical about the fact that our kids may decide to use substances, which we cannot control. And, we can also be firm in our stance that we do not agree with or support this choice. When exploring the cons, we want them to strongly consider that lethality is not worth any short-term reward. When undetectable counterfeit pills or powders are laced, it takes the tiniest amount to kill. We also want to be the ones they call in any situation if they feel discomfort, danger, or if they make a choice of which we disapprove.

Help them cope ahead.

An added value of having these critical conversations about drugs and decision making broadly is to help our kids think and therefore cope ahead. We want them to know how they feel, have a plan (including words they can use), and know when to exit a sketchy situation. Ask them what they think they would do if a close friend offered them a pill. Would they trust it? What can they say that leaves the friendship intact, does not impress judgment, and asserts their boundary? Talk through some different options and help them land with language they feel is authentic to them. Something along the lines of, “Nah dude. I’m good.” Or “No pills, no powders for me.”

Keep the door open and conversations going.

Important topics and evolving independence warrant ongoing conversations. We want our teens and young adults to know we are engaged in their lives, care about what happens to them, and want to talk with them about hard things. Take opportunities to check in when there are reminders, like a recent article, news story, or conversation with other parents. Ask young people what they think about controversial topics and where they get their information. Look with them at different sources, as so much of the news and information they are getting comes from social media. Discuss the difference between fact-checked, vetted sources and editorial commentary. Most of all, remind them, over and over, how much they mean to you, and keep the door open for future discussions.

item.title: Parenting Adolescents and Managing Frustration
item.description:
Adolescence

Parenting Adolescents and Managing Frustration

As the teenager pushes for independence, parents find it harder to get their way.

Posted October 28, 2026

Source: Carl Pickhardt

For many parents, managing a teenager becomes more frustrating than parenting a child.

For example, with the child, parental authority could command compliance: “because I say so!” With the adolescent, parental authority more often has to work for consent: “I’ll listen to your objections if you let me explain my reasons and my need.” With the child, parents could usually order their way. With the adolescent, they more often have to persuade their way.

Parental testimony

A sensitive comment to an earlier blog post (“When parents get angry at their adolescent”) beautifully captured the challenge of this transition. The parent wrote:

“I tend to be fairly patient, but I find myself feeling so frustrated and angry at teenage behavior. I even wake up in the morning just seething — just trying to control the situation, I guess. I just wish I could get it through their head to listen to me. I think one of the biggest frustrations with the teen years, though, is that they also argue rationally! So I can’t win as easily.

Like I might tell my teen ‘you have to wear clean clothes because people will judge you/you could get sick, etc.’ And the teen will argue, ‘but people don’t care about that, and I don’t want people to judge me by my appearance.’ Well fine, but still it makes life harder.

Or, ‘you have to go to sleep at X time’ and [they reply] ‘but I can’t force myself to go to sleep can I?’ It’s like — no, but you have to try. ‘But why try to do something that’s impossible? Are you saying you can just will yourself to sleep?' UGH!

Even though I’ve never thought of myself as an angry person – I’ve been so frustrated lately. It’s become very disruptive to my own well-being, first, and also to my teen's. So, dealing with my own frustration is really important to everyone.”

Yes. It’s easy for parental frustration with not getting one’s own way to create a feeling of anger at being denied that turns into resentment at the denier. And now everyone suffers emotionally.

The danger of frustration

The danger of frustration for parents facing an oppositional teenager is that it can be inflammatory. It can lead to emotional escalation. With more intensity, feelings are increasingly allowed to do parents' "thinking" for them. In this aroused state, parents become more at risk of impulsive and extreme words and actions, while the teenager (because conflict creates resemblance) can feel encouraged by example to ramp up in response. Now each runs the risk of "losing it" to win in the encounter, a bad outcome all the way around.

Should parents find themselves in a state of rising frustration with their teenager, the best advice is: Separate, don't escalate. While the teenager may only be driven to keep going, the parent needs to be motivated to restore calm. So the parent can declare a short time-out, creating a break for both to recover their emotional sobriety, and then re-engage after a specified amount of time when cooler heads can prevail.

Frustration can result from violated expectations

So, what is frustrated when frustration occurs?

The answer often is: expectations. For instance, what you thought would be easy to do or immediately forthcoming proves hard to do or is not occurring. Frustration is the “not getting my way” emotion, a very human felt response to denial, delay, or blockage of three kinds of expectations.

Ambitions: when what a parent wants to happen doesn’t happen. For instance: “I wanted her to remember my birthday, and she forgot it.” Frustration in this case can mean feeling let down. Now the parent can feel inclined to blame the adolescent for disappointing them.

Predictions: when what a parent anticipates will happen doesn’t happen. For instance, “I assumed he’d keep his word and he didn’t." Frustration in this case can mean feeling surprised. Now the parent can feel inclined to blame the adolescent for causing them anxiety.

Conditions: when what a parent believes should happen doesn’t happen. For instance, “She knows the rules and still did wrong.” Frustration in this case can mean feeling betrayed. Now the parent can feel inclined to blame the adolescent for making them angry.

While it's tempting to blame emotional upset from violated parental expectations on the adolescent, it's important for parents to remember that they are responsible for the expectations they set.

Expectations are functional

When an ambition, prediction, or condition is unmet, frustration can result. So does that mean parents shouldn’t have expectations? No. Expectations are functional. They are essential mental sets people depend on to make their way through time and change with some sense of what they would like and what is likely to occur. They are a conceptual bridge to the future to help make the present more manageable. Expectations are one way of thinking ahead.

However, they are mental sets with powerful emotional consequences, particularly when violated. So parents need to choose them carefully. Part of the art of parenting is changing expectations to fit the changing reality of the growing child. Parents who get locked into a childhood set of expectations can find older adolescent behavior very frustrating to live with. Now a lot of normal changes can feel “wrong.”

“She tells us less about herself now.” “He no longer likes to be hugged.” “She prefers time with friends over family.” “He just holes up in his room.” “She spends endless time getting ready to go out.” “He’s more critical of the ways we are.” “She takes forever to do what we ask.” “He’ll argue about the time of day.”

Growing change in the adolescent constantly violates old parental expectations, with adult frustration often being the result. Now a relevant question becomes: “Is my teenager doing something wrong, or are my expectations of teenage behavior out of line?”

The problem with blaming their frustration on the teenager is that parents give that young person control over their emotions. This means they can feel victimized and are more at risk of saying hurtful words in response. But, because expectations are yours to choose, no one can frustrate you without your permission.

Moderating parental frustration

To moderate parental frustration with your adolescent, manage your expectations mindfully.

  • Keep communicating specific expectations for healthy conduct.
  • Keep asking for needed information so you can know what to expect.
  • Treat your expectations as approximations, not absolutes.
  • Adjust your expectations to fit growing adolescent changes.
  • Don’t take violations of expectations as personal affronts.
  • Don’t blame your feelings of frustration on the adolescent.
  • Take emotional responsibility when violated expectations occur.
  • Reset healthy expectations after a violation has been dealt with.

Final words

Consider this scrap of dialogue.

Teenager: “Why do you get angry with me all the time?”

Parent: “Because you’re so frustrating — always doing the unexpected!”

Teenager: “Well, maybe if you expected the unexpected, you’d be less angry.”

Maybe so.

item.title: Why Are We So Obsessed with Elizabeth Holmes?
item.description:
Deception

Why Are We So Obsessed with Elizabeth Holmes?

The crave for justice may drive our fascination with 'You Can See Everything.'

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • The fall of Elizabeth Holmes serves as the ultimate true-crime drama.
  • Seeing the deception unravel satisfies our craving for fairness and accountability.
  • We stay captivated because we want to identify future con-artists before they fool us again.
  • Without an official clinical diagnosis, any psychiatric assessment remains speculative.

Everyone is talking about the new documentary, You Can See Everything. There’s no escaping it. Many armchair psychologists, with or without successful online platforms, are weighing in on what Elizabeth Holmes is truly suffering from. Or, the film often asks, is there no underlying condition at all?

Most prominently, social media has taken to the debate over whether Holmes is on the autism spectrum. It seems evident in the film that perhaps Holmes, her partner, Billy Evans, or maybe even the filmmakers were inferring this as a way to explain some of her unethical behavior and her “neurodivergent” way of communicating her thoughts. In other ways, the film exposes her propensity for lying with no subtlety. Or is she telling the truth?

Viewers scratch their heads. Was the bewilderment a deliberate narrative hoax, or just a story of a fraudster who got exposed? For now, the court of public opinion seems to agree that, if anything, Elizabeth Holmes has undeniable personality disorder traits; this is not a new revelation.

Psychiatric Assessments of Holmes Remain Speculative

However, without an official clinical diagnosis, which we may never get, any psychiatric assessment remains purely speculative. We don’t know.

I have seen both the Alex Gibney HBO documentary, Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley, and You Can See Everything. And after reading John Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: Secret and Lies in a Silicon Valley Startup, the neurodivergent narrative seems like a premeditated ruse. Perhaps it’s a strategic attempt to rebrand her deliberate fraud as communication gaps and blame a mental health condition. Maybe by leaning into the "autistic tech mogul" archetype, she may be fishing for sympathy and trying to rehabilitate her image?

I want to be clear that this is all theoretical. Her behavior appears to resemble traces of narcissism (self-entitlement, the need for admiration), sociopathy (lack of empathy, indifference to causing harm), and a Messiah complex (believing she is destined to save global healthcare).

Her refusal to take accountability for actions that put real lives at risk is true. There is no denying that. But attributing past actions to “thinking differently” than the average person and an inability to process social cues doesn't hold up. She does not seem naive; she can probably distinguish right from wrong. In her mind, she may have had too much to lose, so she doubled down on the fraudulence, even to her own detriment.

Conceivably, Elizabeth Holmes isn't a target of her own mind but a prisoner of her own unrepentant deceptions. Call it neurodivergence if you want, but we don’t have enough hard evidence. Or, a con-artist is just a con-artist.

How Might the Messiah Complex Relate to Holmes?

Another crucial psychological element that is frequently overlooked is the potential Messiah complex:

A Messiah complex is not an official DSM 5 diagnosis. It’s an informal cultural term describing a delusional state characterized by the profound conviction of being divinely chosen to change the world. Elizabeth Holmes often positioned herself as an altruistic visionary destined to save lives. This elevated sense of moral superiority arguably justified unethical behavior, including misleading investors, bypassing safety measures, and ignoring hard facts. Are these delusions of grandeur? Or is it overconfidence?

In Bad Blood, the definitive book that fully unraveled Holmes’ fraud, Wall Street investigative reporter John Carreyrou cited how Holmes required unqualified loyalty from her staff to underpin her deific mission: "If anyone here believes you are not working on the best thing humans have ever built, then you should leave."

When you mix self-absorption, zero remorse, and a savior complex, it creates an explosive dynamic where the hero narrative grants total moral permission to commit fraud, guilt-free. A Messiah complex can stem from grandiose narcissism: an inflated sense of importance, a craving for praise, a need for control, and a disregard for others disguised as self-sacrifice.

Why This Captivates the Public

Finally, you have to wonder why we—including myself—are so infatuated with Elizabeth Holmes and the Theranos crash. Beyond the simple voyeurism of letting cameras into her home before prison, I also see a few other reasons why we are so captivated by this story.

First, there’s the absolute weight of cosmic justice. Holmes completely manipulated military generals, billionaire investors, and media giants. She made fools of them. Watching her face actual prison time proves that no matter how much power and status you accumulate, the truth eventually catches up to everyone.

Also, when the tech industry's "fake it till you make it" attitude starts threatening real lives, seeing that deception unravel satisfies our craving for fairness and accountability. Plus, her massive fall serves as the ultimate true-crime drama, letting us play amateur detectives and satisfying our urge to see wrongdoers held responsible. But in this true-crime drama, the truth finally wins.

In the end, we aren't just staring at a train wreck; we're looking for proof that certainty ultimately prevails over even the craftiest sham. We stay captivated because we want to identify future con artists before they fool us again.

item.title: Your Pain Is Real, But Is It Trauma?
item.description:
Trauma

Your Pain Is Real, But Is It Trauma?

Understanding the difference between trauma and hardship.

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • The definition and understanding of trauma has expanded over time.
  • Calling every hardship traumatic dilutes the meaning of the term.
  • Normal, manageable adversity can foster resilience, strengthen relationships, and build coping skills.
  • Painful experiences don't need a clinical label to be real, valid, and worthy of empathy and support.
Source: Jarle Johansen / Unsplash

Is a child being excluded from a group of friends during a sleepover traumatic? Is getting fired from a job, tripping on the stairs at a conference, being broken up with by a long-term partner, being put on the spot during a meeting, or a parent being late to school pickup traumatic?

Some people will say yes, some will say no, some will argue they need more information, and many will say that they don’t even know what the word “traumatic” means anymore.

The clinical definition of “trauma” has evolved over time, and it now coexists (or perhaps competes) with an increasingly expansive colloquial usage. As a result, we risk overusing this term and thus diminishing its meaning and power.

The definition of “trauma” isn’t as straightforward as one might think. In the DSM-5-TR, a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) requires exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence. This includes directly experiencing an event, witnessing it, or certain forms of indirect exposure, such as learning that a close family member died violently. It’s a necessary criterion that must be met for someone to be diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

However, “trauma” is also used more broadly in psychology to mean an experience that has lasting emotional consequences, even if it doesn’t meet the PTSD criterion. Clinicians sometimes distinguish between “big T” and “little t” traumas, which can make things a tad confusing. “Big T” traumas are the ones we usually think of— fighting in a war, witnessing a life-threatening fight, nearly drowning, etc. “Little t” traumas are experiences that don’t necessarily fit into the DSM’s exposure criteria but can still have significant psychological consequences, especially when they’re repeated or prolonged. They include events like bullying, rejection, or some types of neglect. The extent of impact depends on severity, frequency, and duration of the event(s), as well as the support and resources available to the person.

It’s these “little t” traumas that have muddied the waters. These experiences can cause genuine psychological harm, yes, but the boundaries of what qualifies as traumatic are increasingly difficult to define. We’re having a hard time differentiating psychological harm from psychological trauma. The vagueness has allowed for a rapid expansion of what classifies as a trauma, causing it to become an individually determined label with little room for challenge. Who’s to say that your father having a child with your new stepmother isn’t traumatic if that’s how you feel?

However, life is full of hardships, and not all of them are traumatic. Most of us will get dumped by someone we love, laid off from work, embarrassed in front of friends, devastated by loss, saddened by unwanted change—and that’s okay. A large part of life involves suffering and learning how to get through it. "Trauma" carries a different weight; it suggests that something was distressing, threatening, destabilizing, and possibly life-altering. But something can be distressing and entirely undeserved without being traumatic.

Plus, hardship can have the redeeming quality of creating opportunities for growth. When we navigate manageable adversity, particularly if we have adequate support and resources, we can discover our inner strength, develop resilience, deepen relationships, build coping skills, and develop confidence in our ability to handle future challenges.

There is also a desire to have our pain legitimized by a label. The word “trauma” instantly makes our suffering feel more valid. What we endured wasn’t just “bad,” a word that makes it sound like it could have happened to anyone; it was “traumatic,” a psychological label that conveys an undeniable degree of depth and severity. It’s a word that’s commonly understood to mean something truly devastating. What is this cultural tendency to only view pain as legitimate when it’s clinically significant? Why can’t something simply be painful, humiliating, or heartbreaking without needing it to be traumatic?

However, nobody wants to push back and tell someone their experience wasn’t traumatic. It’s invalidating and would likely embarrass or hurt someone who is trying to communicate the depth of pain they experienced. We don’t want people to become the mental health terminology police, doubting every diagnosis and demanding evidence to justify a label.

At the same time, it’s also not helpful to let every declaration of trauma be considered automatically correct. The word will lose its meaning if it can be used to label any hard or unwanted experience, and we do need a way to distinguish between the painful but manageable events from more serious threats with profound psychological consequences. The severity and impact of a traumatic experience will be diluted if we put performing CPR on an unconscious family member and getting rejected from graduate school in the same category.

Trauma has a clinical meaning, and a colloquial one, which is the case for many psychological terms (e.g., depression and anxiety). We can't eliminate the colloquial use of “trauma,” nor should we regulate and restrict language to that degree. But we can be more mindful of when and how we use it, recognizing that its everyday meaning may differ considerably from the clinical criteria associated with PTSD.

Many painful experiences are things you can navigate, recover from, and integrate into your life. Don’t fall into the trap of calling something traumatic and then viewing your coping or healing as insurmountable. Be mindful of the story you tell yourself about what happened. When we begin to view a painful experience as something that has permanently damaged us, we can underestimate or even limit our capacity to recover, adapt, and move forward.

Preserving the meaning of “trauma” matters, especially for those who have survived profoundly traumatic experiences. Life includes many instances of suffering and, while suffering is painful, it’s not always traumatic. Perhaps the real change we need to make is recognizing that any kind of painful experience is legitimate, even without a clinical label.

item.title: Does Consciousness Need Earth-Made Life?
item.description:
Consciousness

Does Consciousness Need Earth-Made Life?

Could consciousness exist beyond Earth’s biology?

Posted October 28, 2026

Key points
  • Advancements in brain-computer interfaces raise new questions about consciousness and selfhood.
  • Consciousness, as a subjective experience, cannot be directly measured in another mind.
  • Extraterrestrial life may support consciousness on different biological substrates.
  • However, the body, symbiotic microbes, and environment may shape human consciousness.

Elon Musk's courage in driving modern technologies, particularly in combining the brain and computers, should push philosophers to keep pace and address the new issues arising from these advances. It is not surprising that computers and the web will soon be connected with the brain and may become part of its ability. In the case of the brain–computer interface (BCI) and the connection of the brain into a global network, the main question for us is: What will happen to human consciousness? Does this connection to the web make us similar to one another and dissolve our sense of selfhood and identity? With this perspective in mind, we can go even further and ask an old question similar to the question of the Ship of Theseus: If all parts of the brain are gradually replaced with silicon microchips, would consciousness emerge in a silicon brain? This question was first proposed by Tom Cuda and David J. Chalmers as a thought experiment [1,2]. They use this thought experiment to argue that if the functional organization is preserved, conscious experiences must also be preserved.

Let’s look at possible substrates of consciousness. First, we should consider probable consciousness in other living beings on Earth.

1. May other living beings on Earth possess consciousness?

The definition of consciousness is itself controversial among scientists and philosophers. If we define consciousness as a subjective, inner experience, we can better discuss its presence in other species. In this context, it is important to know that we are only sure about our own conscious experiences and do not have direct access to the experiences of others; we can only infer that others have similar experiences. In the philosophy of mind, this can lead to “solipsism,” which is the notion that “I am the only mind that exists,” expressing doubt about the existence of other minds. We must remember that attributing consciousness to other living beings is questionable. Most of the evidence for possible consciousness in other living things is just seeing complex behavior that can be interpreted as conscious experience.

However, Kristin Andrews, Jeff Sebo, and Jonathan Birch, with 39 other neuroscientists, announced on April 19, 2024, at a New York University conference, the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness. They hold that there is strong scientific support for conscious experience in mammals and birds, and at least a realistic possibility that it exists in all vertebrates and many invertebrates, including cephalopods, decapod crustaceans, and insects [3].

2. Possibility of consciousness existence in extraterrestrial life

A recent, interesting paper argues that life beyond Earth need not be based on the same carbon-and-water chemistry as terrestrial life, as some astrobiologists have also hypothesized. The authors estimate that at least 1,000 species exhibiting complex behaviors may have existed, currently exist, or may arise in the universe, potentially with a physicochemical basis different from that of life on Earth. They suggest that some of these species may possess a form of consciousness. They therefore argue that consciousness may emerge from substrates different from those found in humans and other terrestrial species. Their main reasoning involves estimating the number of worlds where life might arise and evolve into species with complex behaviors, given the enormous number of galaxies and stars in the universe.

The authors also use the Copernican principle in their argument, which opposes assuming that humans or life on Earth have a special or unique position in the universe. By applying this principle to consciousness, they concluded that we should not assume that Earth's biological substrate, on which human consciousness depends, is the only one capable of supporting consciousness [4].

Their argument is theoretical and probabilistic rather than based on direct empirical evidence of extraterrestrial consciousness. However, the most important innovation of the article is not simply the claim that consciousness could arise in different materials, but its reframing of the problem. Rather than focusing on the possibility of replacing brain neurons with silicon microchips, the authors ask: In a universe with different evolutionary paths and potentially different chemistries, must consciousness be restricted to a specific biological substrate?

3. Is consciousness linked to life?

Although life itself is a complex concept without a clear definition, many scientists and scholars believe that consciousness is the result of evolutionary processes in living beings. In this context, non-living entities cannot develop conscious experiences. However, some scholars who argue that replacing biological neurons with silicon chips preserves subjective experiences suggest that a robot with a fully silicon-based brain might also develop consciousness, similar to the robotic characters in the series Westworld. Although future advancements may soon reveal the answer to this question, it appears that if we adopt a comprehensive perspective on the formation of consciousness, rather than one focused solely on the brain, we would likely conclude that artificial brains or entities with biochemistries different from our own may not possess consciousness comparable to ours.

One of the authors of the aforementioned paper, Jeremy Pober, contends that while we currently lack sufficient evidence, it is unreasonable to assume that robotic brains and artificial intelligence possess consciousness. But he maintains that consciousness does not require a biological basis. Conversely, another author, Eric Schwitzgebel, adopts a more open-minded stance regarding the possibility of consciousness in AI.

Overall, consciousness is a complex concept with limited consensus regarding its definition. It cannot be measured directly; therefore, scientists infer its presence in an entity by observing indirect changes in brain function or behavior. If we assume that consciousness is a product of the brain alone and ignore the effects of body organs, microbes that live within us symbiotically, environmental factors, and individuals around us, we can propose that it may be found in each living and non-living informational processing system, from an alien with different chemistry to a computer and artificial intelligence. But in a holistic view, humans consist of the body, symbiotic partners, environment, and a biological brain. The integration of bodily and environmental signals by the brain helps to form the consciousness that we know. Therefore, consciousness in other forms of life may differ from our own, particularly if it emerges from a different biological substrate and a different relationship with the body and environment. Understanding such forms of consciousness may be even more difficult for us.
